'''Myōfuku-ji''' (妙福寺) is a {{ill|Nichiren Buddhism|ja|Nichiren宗|1=Nichiren-shū|2=ja|3=日蓮宗|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nichiren Buddhism|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q206611}} temple located in Myōkenchō, Chōshi, Chiba, Japan. Its mountain name (''sangō'') is Kaijōzan. The temple is known for enshrining {{ill|Myōken|en|Myōken|qid=Q10960623|lt=Myōken Bosatsu|1=Myōken}} in its precincts, giving the town its name, and for its famous wisteria trees. The temple’s former main temple affiliation is the Grand Head Temple {{ill|Hokekyō-ji (Ichikawa)|en|Hokekyō-ji (Ichikawa)|qid=Q786113|lt=Hokkekyō-ji|1=Hokekyō-ji (Ichikawa)}}. It belongs to the Oyashi lineage of Nichiren Buddhism.

== History ==
Myōfuku-ji was established on April 26, 1314 (Shōwa 3), by Nikkō, one of Nichiren's direct disciples, with the founding overseen by Nichiyū, the third chief priest of {{ill|Hokekyō-ji (Ichikawa)|en|Hokekyō-ji (Ichikawa)|qid=Q786113|lt=Hokkekyō-ji|1=Hokekyō-ji (Ichikawa)}}.

Originally located in {{ill|Sōsa|en|Sōsa|qid=Q858367|lt=Sōsa|1=Sōsa}}, at a Shingon sect temple in Iriyamasaki, it was converted to the Nichiren sect and relocated to its current site. Construction took approximately 33 years to complete.

The main hall of Myōken Shrine houses a statue of the Great North Star Myōken Bodhisattva, believed to be the first such representation in Japan, attributed to {{ill|Prince Shōtoku|en|Prince Shōtoku|qid=Q263972|lt=Prince Shōtoku|1=Prince Shōtoku}}. The statue was deeply revered by prominent figures such as {{ill|Minamoto no Mitsunaka|en|Minamoto no Mitsunaka|qid=Q2531241|lt=Minamoto no Mitsunaka|1=Minamoto no Mitsunaka}}, who passed it down through the Minamoto clan. Later, figures like {{ill|Minamoto no Yoritomo|en|Minamoto no Yoritomo|qid=Q242800|lt=Minamoto no Yoritomo|1=Minamoto no Yoritomo}} and {{ill|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|en|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|qid=Q187550|lt=Toyotomi Hideyoshi|1=Toyotomi Hideyoshi}} also revered it. During the Edo period, it was transferred from Edo Castle to the Matsudaira family, rulers of Takō Castle. In 1715 (Shōtoku 5), it was enshrined at Myōfuku-ji through the efforts of various benefactors, including the Matsudaira family and the Tokugawa shogunate.

A prior chief abbot, Hirono Nichii Shōnin, ascended to become the 143rd chief priest of the Grand Head Temple, Hokkekyō-ji.
